To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SOCS genes, which are known as negative regulators of the JAK/STAT signaling pathways, are constitutively expressed in human breast-cancer cells and are differentially regulated by IFNγ.
the expression of SOCS1, SOCS2, and SOCS3 in MCF- 7 breast-cancer cell is differentially regulated by proinflammatory cytokin IFNγ and trophic factor IGF-1.
SOCS genes expression is constitutively up-regulated in breast-cancer and prostate cancer cells, suggesting a potential mechanism of resistance of these cancers to IFNγ and other cytokines.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of SOCS genes as negative regulators of cytokine and trophic factor signaling in the mammary epithelium and the potential contribution of aberrant SOCS expression in breast-cancer development.
the role of SOCS proteins in the development of human breast cancer.
understanding the mechanisms that regulate SOCS genes and the role of SOCS genes as tumor suppressors and/or oncogenes in human epithelial cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SOCS genes expression is not silenced by epigenetic mechanism in the breast-cancer cells examined in this study.

the SOCS genes are differentially regulated in normal and cancer cells, and that the expression of SOCS1 gene in breast cancer cells is up-regulated by proinflammatory cytokinies and radiation, but not by trophic factors.

, while SOCS1 gene is transcriptionally silenced in some human cancers, SOCS1 and other SOCS genes are constitutively up-regulated by epigenetic mechanisms in breast cancer cells, and may confer resistance to IFNγ and other cytokine signaling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SOCS genes expression is differentially regulated by cytokine and growth factors signals in breast-cancer and prostate-cancer cells, but not in normal breast cells.
SOCS genes in normal mammary epithelial cells are regulated by the STAT5 pathway, while in breast-cancer cell SOCS genes are constitutively expressed by the STAT3 pathways.

the SOCS gene expression is not epigenetically silenced by DNA-hypermethylated in breast and prostate cancers and the SOCS genes are constitutively expressed in cancer cells at a level comparable to or higher than that in normal epithelial cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SOCS genes may play a role in the development and/or progression of breast-cancer.

the expression of SOCS1, SOCS3 and SOCS5 is constitutively upregulated in human breast cancer cells and that the expression of these genes in breast-cancers cells may not be regulated by the epigenomic mechanism of DNA-hypermethylation.

the SOCS genes in cancer cells are not silenced by DNA-hypermethylated and are not functionally defective, and that the SOCS proteins in these cells are likely to be active and may contribute to oncogenic transformation by inhibiting the proapoptotic and antiproliferative activities of IFNγ and other cytokines.
